newsitem.title: USA: White House says Clinton will veto abortion bill.
newsitem.headline: White House says Clinton will veto abortion bill.

text.p: On the eve of debate on a bill to ban a controversial abortion procedure, the White House Wednesday said the measure contained "serious flaws" and warned Congress President Clinton would veto it.
A new measure to ban so-called partial birth abortions was introduced in the House earlier this month and will be debated Thursday.
Clinton vetoed a proposed ban on the procedure last April, but said he would sign such a prohibition if it included an exception for cases where the woman's health was at risk.
The White House said in a written statement the new bill contained "the same serious flaws" as the one approved by Congress last year and announced Clinton would veto it for the same reasons.

"By refusing to permit women, in reliance on their doctors' best medical judgment, to use this procedure when their lives are threatened or when their health is put in serious jeopardy, the Congress has fashioned a bill that is consistent neither with the Constitution nor with sound public policy," Clinton said in his 1996 veto message.
The procedure involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.
The issue has sparked heated debate, with abortion rights proponents faulting the proposed ban as unconstitutional and abortion foes calling the procedure itself barbaric.

Ron Fitzsimmons, executive director of the National Coalition of Abortion Providers, re-ignited the controversy recently by saying he "lied through my teeth" when he defended this kind of late-term abortion.
Instead of the 500 or so a year cited by abortion rights activists, he said as many as 5,000 might be performed, many on women in earlier stages of non-crisis pregnancies.

Clinton, whose overall position on abortion has been that it should be safe, legal and rare, argued that the procedure was performed on only a few hundred women whose health was endangered or whose foetuses had terrible deformities.

After Fitzsimmons' disclosure and the re-introduction of the bill in Congress, Clinton said any law on the contentious issue should ensure that the procedure remained available to the few women who truly needed it.

"I think you could make a very compelling case that for the small number of people I'm trying to protect, this is the biggest issue in their entire lives and that for them my position is pro-life," he said.
